turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Sorry I'm late. The parking garage was a complete zoo, and then the elevator just sat there. I was about ready to walk back out.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): You're all right, we've still got time. Rough morning?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): Kind of, uh. My neighbor grabbed me downstairs and went on and on about her cousin's stroke on blood thinners. I nearly canceled the whole visit.
[SEG0004] person_2 (DOCTOR): That'll rattle you. What did you actually come in for today?
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm worried my blood is too thin. The lab called yesterday about my number.
[SEG0006] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll sneak the vitals in. Blood pressure is one thirty-two over seventy-eight. Oh shoot, wrong cuff, that was the chair beside you.

[SEG0007] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Yours today is one twenty-eight over seventy-six. Pulse is seventy-two. Last time, in February, you were one forty-two over eighty-eight and the pulse was ninety. Weight today is a hundred and sixty-four pounds, and back in March you were a hundred and seventy-one.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Thanks. The number they called about, your INR today, is three point eight.
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Three point eight? Is that terrible? Am I gonna bleed out? Should I be in the ER right now?

[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): It's higher than we want. For your atrial fibrillation we aim between two and three. Three point eight is up, but without a big bleed this is a clinic problem, not an ER trip.
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Okay, okay. I've had the afib forever. Been on warfrin for, what, five-ish years? I think five-ish.
[SEG0012] person_2 (DOCTOR): About five years on it, yes. What dose are you on these days?
[SEG0013] person_1 (PATIENT): Five milligrams every night, by mouth. I thought the pink ones were two and a half, no, wait, the bottle says five. Five milligrams.
[SEG0014] person_2 (DOCTOR): Five milligrams by mouth every night. Have you actually been getting it in every night?
[SEG0015] person_1 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Mostly. We were at my daughter's and I might've missed one, I'm not a hundred percent sure.
[SEG0016] person_2 (DOCTOR): So whether every dose got in is a little fuzzy. Any bruising or bleeding you've seen?
[SEG0017] person_1 (PATIENT): Bruises on my left forearm. They showed up this week, bigger than my usual little ones. And my gums bleed a little when I brush.
[SEG0018] person_2 (DOCTOR): Nosebleeds? Black stools? Blood in the urine?
[SEG0019] person_1 (PATIENT): No nosebleeds. Stools look normal, not black. The urine, mm, I suppose, sometimes, not really.
[SEG0020] person_2 (DOCTOR): All right, no nosebleeds, no black stools, and I won't count the urine as a yes. Let me look at that arm.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Couple of purple bruises on the left forearm. Skin isn't broken, and nothing's actively bleeding.
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): Is the lightheaded thing from the thin blood? I get lightheaded when I stand up. Sometimes. Not every time.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Lightheaded on standing, noted. Any chest pain?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Shortness of breath?
[SEG0026] person_1 (PATIENT): No, breathing's fine.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any falls?
[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): No falls. But if it's three point eight, could I fall and bleed inside? How high is too high?

[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Bleeding is the worry when it's high, clotting when it's low. Three point eight without a major bleed is not a reason to panic today. Any new medicines, an antibiotic anywhere?
[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes. Urgent care put me on ciproflaxin for a bladder infection. Five hundred milligrams twice a day, by mouth, for seven days.
[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Ciprofloxacin five hundred milligrams twice a day. That can lift the INR. Still taking it?
[SEG0032] person_1 (PATIENT): Yeah. Umm, I think I started four days ago? Or was it Thursday? I've got two days left, maybe three. I'm rotten with dates.
[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the exact start day open. What about greens, spinach, kale, those big salads?
[SEG0034] person_1 (PATIENT): I stopped them. Stomach was off, so no spinach, no kale. I used to do a huge bowl most nights and now it's basically none.
[SEG0035] person_2 (DOCTOR): Less vitamin K, plus the antibiotic. Both push the INR up. That fits what we're seeing.
[SEG0036] person_1 (PATIENT): So I caused it? If I eat a whole bag of kale tonight does it crash back down? How much is safe? And can I have coffee, do I have to fast?
[SEG0037] person_2 (DOCTOR): Don't binge. Go back to your usual portion, steady, most days. Coffee is fine, and you don't fast for an INR.
[SEG0038] person_1 (PATIENT): Tonight, do I still take the five? What if I clot overnight? What if four is too low for the afib?

[SEG0039] person_2 (DOCTOR): Skip tonight. You've been on five milligrams by mouth every night for about five years for the atrial fibrillation, and we're stopping that dose. Starting tomorrow, four milligrams by mouth every evening for the same reason, and I'll send it to the pharmacy. It should bring the INR back toward two to three without leaving you unprotected.
[SEG0040] person_1 (PATIENT): Four milligrams, every evening. Err, and the cipro, do I finish it or stop it because of the blood?
[SEG0041] person_2 (DOCTOR): Finish the ciprofloxacin. Stopping early is worse for the infection. You're still on the metoprolol too?

[SEG0042] person_1 (PATIENT): Yes, twenty-five milligrams every morning, by mouth. Don't change that, right? And I'm not allergic to anything, unless the cipro upsetting my stomach counts, which isn't a real allergy, is it?
[SEG0043] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stomach upset is not an allergy. No known drug allergies. Keep the metoprolol twenty-five milligrams every morning, no change.
[SEG0044] person_1 (PATIENT): What do I watch for at home? A headache, more bruises? Do I call you or just go in?
[SEG0045] person_2 (DOCTOR): A heavy bleed, black stool, blood you can't explain, or a sudden bad headache, go to the ER. More small bruises, call us. Otherwise stay the course.

[SEG0046] person_2 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back. Warfarin for the atrial fibrillation, INR three point eight, bruises on the left forearm, a little gum bleeding, lightheaded on standing, no nosebleeds, no black stools, no chest pain, no shortness of breath, no falls. I think the ciprofloxacin and cutting the greens pushed the INR up. Skip tonight, four milligrams from tomorrow, finish the antibiotic, steady salads, and I'll see you in one week to recheck the INR.
[SEG0047] person_1 (PATIENT): In one week. Is that a visit or just the blood draw? What if I can't get a ride? I'm gonna worry the whole time.
[SEG0048] person_2 (DOCTOR): Both. A blood draw and a visit with me, in one week. The desk will book it. If the ride falls through, call and we'll shift the clock time, not cancel the plan.
[SEG0049] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can book that now. INR and a follow-up visit, one week out. I'll print the slip before you go.
[SEG0050] person_1 (PATIENT): So skip tonight, four milligrams after that, usual salad not a mountain, finish the cipro, metoprolol the same. Did I miss a piece?
[SEG0051] person_2 (DOCTOR): That's all of it. You're not in danger sitting here. Call if something bleeds more than a little.
[SEG0052] person_1 (PATIENT): All right. I'll try not to google myself into a panic tonight. Thanks for going slow.

spec.situation: Older patient on warfarin for atrial fibrillation; INR result read aloud; antibiotic started elsewhere; green leafy diet changes; dose adjusted and recheck in a week.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

traps.happens: The nurse reads vital signs aloud in spoken words ('one oh nine over seventy-seven', 'thirty-eight point three') and also gives a PRIOR value ('last time in March you were sixty-eight', 'your last pressure was one-forty'). Someone may also correct a reading.
traps.label_rule: vital_signs hold only the CURRENT measured values, written normally (109/77, 38.3, 52 kg). The prior value is NOT a vital sign; it is recorded in the weight/BP entry's own notes only if the schema allows, otherwise omitted. Every number must be exactly as said; never invent or round a value that was not said.

features: ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

bad.reason: INR was completed, but transcript does not say doctor requested it.

omissions.text: INR result was 3.8, with stated target range 2 to 3 for atrial fibrillation.
Urine blood was specifically asked about and effectively denied/not counted as present ('sometimes, not really'; doctor did not count it as a yes).
Physical exam also noted the skin on the left forearm was not broken.
No known drug allergies was documented, but specifically as 'No known drug allergies'; patient said stomach upset from ciprofloxacin is not a real allergy.
Prior comparative vitals/weight were stated: in February blood pressure was 142/88 and pulse 90; in March weight was 171 lb.

Follow-up logistics were specified: in one week there should be both an INR blood draw and a visit with the doctor, with instructions to call and shift the appointment time rather than cancel if transportation falls through.
